clue.text: Airborne beadle

parts.note: Mr Bumble is the parish beadle in Dickens's Oliver Twist; give him wings and he becomes a buzzing insect

explanation.walkthrough: Mr Bumble is the pompous beadle (a parish officer) in Dickens's Oliver Twist; a Bumble that flies is the furry insect.
explanation.definitionFit: The insect is a large hairy bee that flies, and Bumble is the name of Dickens's beadle.

clue.text: Bill's among the press men in Lancs

indicators.note: the account sits among the letters standing for the press agency, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: BUP was British United Press, a news agency
a bill is an account, abbreviated AC

explanation.surface: An invoice turns up among the newspaper reporters somewhere in the north.
explanation.walkthrough: Lancs is short for Lancashire, an English county, and the definition is a town there. British United Press was a news agency, and 'among' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Bacup is a small mill town in the Rossendale valley of Lancashire.

clue.text: Mum rules the city

parts.note: mum is mother, informally MA
ruled lines on paper are rules

explanation.surface: Mother lays down the law for the whole town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rules' looks like a verb, but it is the noun: ruled lines on paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Malines is the French name of Mechelen, a Belgian city famous for lace.

clue.text: Chief of the main properties of Scott's poetry

definitions.text: Chief of the main properties of Scott's poetry

parts.words: Chief of the main properties of Scott's poetry
parts.note: a ruler whose possessions lie out in the sea, which is also the title of a long narrative poem by Walter Scott

explanation.walkthrough: 'the main' is the sea, so its properties are islands; the title was held by Scottish chiefs and Scott wrote a poem of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: The title belonged to the medieval Macdonald chiefs of the Hebrides and names Walter Scott's 1815 poem.

clue.text: He may have to use his loaf to get it

definitions.text: He may have to use his loaf to get it

parts.words: He may have to use his loaf to get it
parts.note: using your loaf means thinking, and the earner of the household brings home the bread

explanation.walkthrough: 'Use your loaf' is British slang for 'think' (loaf of bread = head, rhyming slang); the person who earns the family's bread must think hard to get it.
explanation.definitionFit: The family member whose wages keep the household is the one who earns the daily bread.

clue.text: Er — guvner, can you spare a dyne to get a bit of work ?

indicators.note: the beggar asks for a share of something, and here a share of the opening word is handed over

explanation.surface: A beggar asks a toff for a coin so as to start working.
explanation.walkthrough: The start of 'Er-guvner' holds the answer; 'a dyne' is a pun on 'a dime', and one dyne acting through one centimetre does exactly this much work.
explanation.definitionFit: The erg is the old centimetre-gram-second unit of work or energy, a very small amount.

clue.text: Add 'em up to get this figure

parts.note: to tot up is to add up a column of numbers
the clipped form of them, written without its apostrophe

explanation.surface: An instruction to total the numbers and arrive at a sum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' just completes the phrase 'tot up'. 'figure' looks like a number, but it is a carved image.
explanation.definitionFit: A totem is a carved or painted emblem, as on a totem pole, so a sculpted image.

clue.text: Company liquidator

parts.note: the saying runs two's company, three's a crowd, so the extra arrival ends the company

explanation.walkthrough: Not a business winding-up: 'two's company, three's a crowd', so the newcomer who makes it three dissolves the company.
explanation.definitionFit: One more person after a pair is the number three in line, the unwanted extra.

clue.text: I'm among damaged paint drums

indicators.note: the clue word I'm sits among the other letters, so it goes inside them
something damaged is knocked out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, without its apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone stands amid spoiled paint pots, banging percussion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'damaged' signals the anagram of the paint, and 'among' sets the clue's I'm inside it, just after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Timpani are kettledrums, the large tuned drums of an orchestra.

clue.text: Three causes of a guest's late arrival at Forres

definitions.text: Three causes of a guest's late arrival at Forres

parts.words: Three causes of a guest's late arrival at Forres
parts.note: in Macbeth, Banquo is killed on the road and appears at the feast at Forres only as a ghost

explanation.walkthrough: 'late' means dead: Macbeth hires three men to kill Banquo before the banquet at Forres, where his ghost turns up.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Macbeth lists three hired killers among its characters, and they are the ones who ambush Banquo.

clue.text: California, if not, one goes east for a bit of warmth

parts.note: or means if not, as in 'hurry or you'll be late'
the Roman numeral I is one
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A traveller weighs up California against heading east for some sun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes' only joins I to E.
explanation.definitionFit: The calorie is a unit of heat energy, a small measured quantity of warmth.

clue.text: Not much intelligence, moony

definitions.meaning: a faint trace of understanding, as in a flicker of an idea
pale and faintly shining, as the moon does

explanation.surface: A dreamy person is described as not very bright.
explanation.definitionFit: A faint first understanding is a mere flicker of it; the moon gives only a dim, wavering light.

clue.text: Ape in khaki

definitions.meaning: a great ape, from an old genus name
a soldier, since army uniform is khaki; old naval slang for one

explanation.surface: A monkey dressed in army uniform.
explanation.definitionFit: Pongo was the old genus name for the great apes, now the orang-utans; sailors' slang called a soldier a pongo.

clue.text: To do this, get the hay-tedder busy

definitions.text: To do this, get the hay-tedder busy

indicators.note: a busy machine is all action, so these letters are stirred about

explanation.surface: Advice to a farmer: set the haymaking machine going to dry the crop.
explanation.walkthrough: A hay-tedder turns cut hay so it dries; 'busy' rearranges HAYTEDDER, and the whole clue says what the machine does.
explanation.definitionFit: Tedding spreads hay out to dry, removing its water, which is the action meant.

clue.text: Anything but easy-going as a rule

definitions.meaning: the phrase usually describes a rule that admits no exceptions

explanation.surface: A strict person is seldom relaxed, generally speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: Something rigid and fixed is the opposite of relaxed, and the phrase is an idiom for a strict rule.

clue.text: On this side, Cicely ?

definitions.meaning: the Latin prefix for this side of, as in cisalpine
a pet form of the girl's name

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether Cicely is on our team.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin prefix meaning 'on this side' (as in cisalpine) is also a pet form of the girl's name Cicely.

clue.text: Outsize millinery bill added to other debts ?

parts.note: millinery is hats, and a cap is one
a bill is an account, abbreviated AC
IOUs are written promises to pay, so debts

explanation.surface: A huge hat bill piles on top of everything else owed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outsize' looks like a description of the hat, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something roomy that holds a great deal is vast in size.

clue.text: The narrowness of many a British victory in the past

definitions.text: The narrowness of many a British victory in the past

parts.words: The narrowness of many a British victory in the past
parts.note: narrowness is a slender scarlet-coated line of soldiers rather than a slim margin of victory

explanation.walkthrough: A narrow victory is usually a close one; here the narrowness is the thin line of red-coated British infantry, famously at Balaclava in 1854.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the redcoat infantry line holding off cavalry at Balaclava, and by extension the British army.

clue.text: Architectural feature of the White Rabbit's disappearance

definitions.meaning: a slit window in a tower or steeple
in Alice in Wonderland, a dream, the White Rabbit vanishes down a rabbit burrow

explanation.surface: A building detail inspired by the rabbit vanishing in Alice in Wonderland.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a slit opening in a tower wall for light; in Alice's dream the White Rabbit vanishes down a burrow.

clue.text: Port for Sally

parts.note: a sally port is a small gate in a castle wall for soldiers to rush out through, not a drink for a girl

explanation.walkthrough: Port here is a gateway (Latin porta), not wine, and a sally is a sudden sortie by besieged troops, not a girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A small back entrance in a fortification served as the sally port for sorties.

clue.text: He is often helpful to inquiring police

definitions.text: He is often helpful to inquiring police

parts.words: He is often helpful to inquiring police
parts.note: the press phrase says a man is helping police with their inquiries, the polite way of saying they think he did it

explanation.walkthrough: British news reports say a man 'is helping police with their inquiries', meaning he is under suspicion.
explanation.definitionFit: The person helping with inquiries in the press phrase is in fact the one the police think guilty.

clue.text: Reverse, silly, in the dance

indicators.note: the instruction at the front tells us to read the next word's synonym backwards

parts.note: a silly person is a sap, a fool

explanation.surface: A dancing instruction to back up, foolishly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reverse' turns SAP round; the definition is a step in ballet.
explanation.definitionFit: Pas is the French ballet term for a step, a single movement in dancing.

clue.text: Clip 'im, love, anyway in SW1

indicators.note: anyway means in any order at all, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: love is nil in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: A gangster orders someone knocked about in a smart London district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyway' rearranges CLIPIM to PIMLIC. SW1 is the postcode of central Westminster in London, which includes this district.
explanation.definitionFit: Pimlico is a district of central London lying in the SW1 postal area.

clue.text: Sacked for rifling the till ?

definitions.meaning: dismissed from the armed forces in disgrace
read as ..., someone has been at the cash

explanation.surface: An employee is fired for stealing money from the shop till.
explanation.definitionFit: Being dismissed in disgrace from service is the usual sense, and the word also looks like the cash in a till being taken.

clue.text: See 3
Oh god, why is mum so ridiculous ?

indicators.note: something ridiculous is absurdly put together, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in exasperation at how silly their mother is being.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oh' and 'why is' are surface padding; 'ridiculous' rearranges MUMSO.
explanation.definitionFit: Momus was the Greek god of mockery and satire, a deity of ridicule.

clue.text: It may be a bit of a shock

definitions.text: It may be a bit of a shock

parts.words: It may be a bit of a shock
parts.note: a shock of corn is a stook, a pile of bound bundles stood together in a field, not a fright

explanation.walkthrough: A shock is a stook of corn: several bound bundles stood upright in a harvest field, so one bundle is part of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A bound bundle of cut corn stalks is one of the units stacked into a stook.

clue.text: Encroach so one might get slated

definitions.meaning: roof slates are laid with each covering part of the next

explanation.surface: Trespassing might get one criticised.
explanation.definitionFit: To extend over something else is to intrude on it; roof tiles are laid so each covers part of the one below.

clue.text: Where landlordism is barred

parts.note: the landlord here serves behind a bar, so his trade happens over a counter rather than being banned

explanation.walkthrough: 'barred' looks like 'banned'; it means done behind a bar, where the landlord of a British tavern serves drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: A British tavern is run by a landlord who serves from behind the bar.

clue.text: " Dream ? strive to do, and —— to do, And fail in doing " (Browning)

definitions.text: Dream ? strive to do, and —— to do, And fail in doing " (Browning)

parts.words: Dream ? strive to do, and —— to do, And fail in doing " (Browning)
parts.note: a quotation from Browning's Andrea del Sarto with one word missing, the verb of painful struggle

explanation.walkthrough: The page prints a dash for the gap after 'and'. The line is from Browning's poem Andrea del Sarto: the missing verb means to struggle in anguish.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap needs a verb of anguished effort, between striving and failing, in Browning's line about painters.

clue.text: Tess and I change places

indicators.note: to change these letters is to swap them about into a new order

explanation.surface: Two people, Tess and the speaker, swap seats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'places' looks part of 'change places', but it is the definition; 'change' rearranges TESSI.
explanation.definitionFit: Locations or positions where things stand are their sites.

clue.text: Richer when not working ?

definitions.meaning: wealthier, in a more comfortable position
read as better plus off, an idle state, the phrase suggests it is preferable not to work

explanation.surface: Someone muses that they would have more money if they stopped going to work.
explanation.definitionFit: Having more money is being wealthier, and a machine switched off and idle is in a better state of rest.
